justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across all three horizons, starting near 112.5 for the one-day forecast and gradually rising to 114.5 at one month. This trajectory assumes a baseline continuation of recent price momentum or fair-value drift, without assuming any major catalysts. The one-day estimate is anchored closely to the last observed price level, with only a small expected move reflecting typical intraday mean reversion and low overnight drift. The one-week and one-month estimates incorporate a slight positive bias, consistent with a modest trend or carry assumption, but the incremental increase is deliberately small because I have no strong directional conviction beyond the near term.

The confidence interval widths expand meaningfully as the horizon lengthens, which reflects the standard square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty combined with event risk accumulating over longer windows. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 7 points, capturing normal daily volatility. By one week, the interval widens to 14 points, incorporating the possibility of a macro surprise, earnings release, or sentiment shift. At one month, the interval stretches to 29 points, reflecting the compounding of weekly uncertainties plus the realistic possibility of a regime change — a shift in monetary policy expectations, a geopolitical development, or a broader risk-off episode that could materially reprice the asset.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected economic data print, a dovish central bank pivot, or a short-squeeze dynamic could push prices well above 129 at the one-month horizon. On the downside, a credit event, a sharp deterioration in liquidity, or an unexpected hawkish surprise could drive prices below 100. These tail events are not fully captured even in a 90% interval, meaning there is still a residual 10% probability of outcomes beyond those bounds — and in practice, fat-tailed financial distributions mean the true tail risk may be somewhat larger than a normal-distribution assumption would suggest.

It is also worth acknowledging that my estimates carry model uncertainty on top of market uncertainty. The point estimates and intervals were constructed using general heuristics about volatility scaling and drift, rather than a calibrated model fitted to this specific asset's historical behavior. If this asset exhibits mean reversion, the upward drift assumption may be too generous; if it exhibits momentum, the drift may be too conservative. Users should treat these forecasts as a rough probabilistic scaffold rather than a precise quantitative prediction.
